extracted.intended_audience: general public and public health stakeholders
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and recommended actions for schools, workplaces, clinicians, and the public during the 2009 H1N1 pandemic, covering infection control, quarantine, treatment, surveillance, and health-system surge preparations.

rubrics_metrics.name: School exclusion period for symptomatic persons
rubrics_metrics.description: Students and school workers with flu symptoms should stay home for either seven days total, or until 24 hours after symptoms subsided, whichever was longer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CDC recommended this instead of blanket school closures; applied to enforce self-isolation and reduce transmission among school-age populations (which were disproportionately affected).

rubrics_metrics.name: Colleges consider suspending classes if severe illness increases
rubrics_metrics.description: Colleges should consider suspending fall classes if the virus begins to cause severe illness in a significantly larger share of students than previously observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a situational, data-driven decision recommended by the CDC rather than an automatic closure policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspend punitive academic policies to enable self-isolation
rubrics_metrics.description: Schools were urged to suspend rules such as penalties for late papers or missed classes and requirements for a doctor's note to enforce 'self-isolation' and prevent students from venturing out while ill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy flexibility (leniency on penalties/documentation) is recommended to reduce disincentives to stay home.

rubrics_metrics.name: On-site isolation room for symptomatic individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Schools were advised to set aside a room for people developing flu-like symptoms while they waited to go home.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ill students or staff and those caring for them were also advised to use face masks while in that space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stockpiling and contingency planning for school closures
rubrics_metrics.description: Schools/universities were advised to stockpile supplies (masks, sanitiser, food, water) and plan for worst-case scenarios, including providing lessons and meals for low-income children if schools closed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include University of California campuses stockpiling masks and sanitizer; plans should consider vulnerable populations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local 'influenza action team' formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendation that every county should create an 'influenza action team' run by the local health department, parents, and school administrators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested by a Pediatrics professor to coordinate local preparedness and response among stakeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employer pandemic planning objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers should consider and communicate objectives such as reducing transmission among staff, protecting people at increased risk of complications, maintaining business operations, and minimising adverse effects on supply chains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: HHS/CDC/DHS issued guidance and employer-focused materials (including a video) to help develop workplace pandemic plans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workforce absenteeism planning and remote work readiness
rubrics_metrics.description: The CDC estimated that as much as 40% of the workforce might be unable to work at the peak; individuals and employers should have steps in place should a workplace close or remote work be required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plans should include contingencies for childcare, business continuity, and remote-work arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workplace exclusion period for sick employees
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons in the workplace should stay home sick for seven days after getting the flu, or 24 hours after symptoms end, whichever is longer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Same operational standard as school exclusion guidance; intended to limit workplace transmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: General employer guidance (UK HSE reference)
rubrics_metrics.description: The UK's Health and Safety Executive issued general guidance for employers on responding to pandemic influenza.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes HSE guidance existed but does not reproduce detailed criteria in this excerpt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mask use in non-healthcare settings (CDC recommendation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The U.S. CDC did not recommend the use of face masks or respirators in non-health care settings (schools, workplaces, public places), with exceptions for people who were ill when around others and people at risk for severe illness while caring for someone with the flu.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mask use was recommended selectively for source control (ill persons) and for caregivers at risk; widespread public use was not advised by CDC at the time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat about masks giving false security
rubrics_metrics.description: Some experts feared that masks may give people a false sense of security and should not replace other standard precautions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Masks are 'better than nothing' per some virologists but cannot completely block airborne virus transmission through gaps; masks should not replace hand hygiene, isolation, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacturer statement on mask effectiveness for biological agents
rubrics_metrics.description: 3M stated masks will filter out particles in industrial settings, but 'there are no established exposure limits for biological agents such as swine flu virus'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manufacturers distinguish industrial particulate filtration from proven protection against infectious biological agents; this limits claims about expected protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural uptake of masks despite limited evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Despite lack of evidence of effectiveness, the use of such masks is common in Asia and particularly popular in Japan, where etiquette obligates those who are sick to wear masks to avoid spreading disease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultural norms may drive mask adoption even when epidemiological evidence is limited; public messaging must consider cultural factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quarantine of suspected infected visitors
rubrics_metrics.description: Countries initiated or threatened quarantines of foreign visitors suspected of having or being in contact with infected persons; e.g., China confined students, Hong Kong quarantined a hotel, Australia held a cruise ship at sea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quarantine and travel restrictions were used as public health tools; such measures prompted travel alerts (e.g., US State Department) and international concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Food safety guidance regarding pork
rubrics_metrics.description: Leading health agencies and agriculture officials stressed that eating properly cooked pork or other food products derived from pigs will not cause flu.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public communication emphasized food safety to counteract stigma and prevent unnecessary trade/consumption disruptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government trade/trade-restriction responses to outbreak
rubrics_metrics.description: Some governments imposed bans on importation of animal products, halted pig imports, examined pig populations, or ordered culling (examples: Azerbaijan ban, Indonesia examinations, Egypt slaughtered pigs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are government policy responses taken despite health agencies' food-safety assurances; they illustrate political/economic measures in outbreaks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symptomatic self-care recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommended methods to help ease symptoms include adequate fluid intake and rest; over-the-counter pain medications (paracetamol, ibuprofen) may reduce symptoms but do not kill the virus; aspirin and other salicylates should not be used by people under 16 due to Reye syndrome risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If fever is mild and no complications, fever medication is not recommended. Most people recover without medical attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antiviral treatment priority for at-risk groups
rubrics_metrics.description: People in at-risk groups (pregnant and postpartum women, children under two years old, and people with underlying conditions such as respiratory problems) should be treated with antivirals (oseltamivir or zanamivir) as soon as possible when symptoms start.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early treatment is emphasized for groups at higher risk of complications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antiviral use for worsening illness and pneumonia
rubrics_metrics.description: People not in at-risk groups who have persistent or rapidly worsening symptoms should also be treated with antivirals; people who have developed pneumonia should be given both antivirals and antibiotics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combining antivirals and antibiotics is common in severe cases where bacterial infection is suspected; clinical judgment required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antiviral timing effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Antivirals are most useful if given within 48 hours of the start of symptoms; in those beyond 48 hours who are moderately or severely ill, antivirals may still be beneficial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early administration maximizes benefit, but treatment can be considered later in severe cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitute antiviral recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: If oseltamivir (Tamiflu) is unavailable or cannot be used, zanamivir (Relenza) is recommended as a substitute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternative agents should be considered based on availability and patient suitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of experimental antivirals for hospitalized patients
rubrics_metrics.description: Peramivir is an experimental antiviral drug approved for hospitalized patients in cases where the other available methods of treatment are ineffective or unavailable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental/less-proven agents may be reserved for severe/hospitalized patients when standard antivirals are unsuitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritization of antiviral use to avoid shortages
rubrics_metrics.description: To help avoid shortages, the U.S. CDC recommended oseltamivir treatment primarily for people hospitalized with pandemic flu; people at risk of serious flu complications; and patients at risk of serious flu complications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve limited antiviral supplies for those most likely to benefit to reduce risk of shortage and preserve efficacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of antiviral resistance from indiscriminate use
rubrics_metrics.description: The CDC warned that indiscriminate use of antiviral medications to prevent and treat influenza could ease the way for drug-resistant strains to emerge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rational, prioritized use of antivirals is needed to limit selection for resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patient adherence concerns with antiviral courses
rubrics_metrics.description: A British report found that people often failed to complete a full course of the drug or took the medication when not needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-adherence and inappropriate use undermine effectiveness and may promote resistance; public education is important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Known side effects and pediatric concerns for antivirals
rubrics_metrics.description: Oseltamivir and zanamivir have known side effects (lightheadedness, chills, nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite, trouble breathing); children were reported to be at increased risk of self-injury and confusion after taking oseltamivir.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clinicians should weigh benefits and risks, particularly for pediatric patients, and monitor for neuropsychiatric adverse events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning against purchasing antivirals from unverified online sources
rubrics_metrics.description: The WHO warned against buying antiviral medications from online sources and estimated that half the drugs sold by online pharmacies without a physical address were counterfeit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use verified pharmacies and national medical supply chains to avoid counterfeit or substandard medications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surveillance role and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Influenza surveillance answers where, when, and what influenza viruses are circulating and is crucial for response (e.g., sharing genetic sequences via GISAID), but surveillance cannot be used to ascertain how many people have become ill with influenza.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surveillance data are essential for tracking viral evolution and outbreaks but are limited in estimating total case counts due to under-ascertainment and testing biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Death count estimation caveat
rubrics_metrics.description: Influenza is infrequently listed on death certificates of people who die from flu-related complications; counting only deaths where influenza was listed would be a gross underestimation of influenza's true impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epidemiological methods and modelling are needed to estimate excess mortality attributable to influenza beyond certificate counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shift in WHO case-counting focus during epidemic
rubrics_metrics.description: During the outbreak the WHO stopped keeping count of individual cases and focused more on monitoring major outbreaks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counting every case can be misleading and resource-intensive; surveillance emphasis may shift to clusters and severity indicators in widespread pandemics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hospital surge-capacity preparedness measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Hospitals increased ED surge capacities by repurposing spaces (lobby as waiting area), using outpatient facilities during off-hours, utilizing short-stay units for longer care, employing non-board certified physicians and inpatient nurses for ED care, transforming other units into ED rooms, and expanding single-patient rooms to multiple beds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple operational adaptations can expand capacity quickly; planning should include staff cross-deployment, space reconfiguration, and alternate care sites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative severity and affected demographics
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2009 H1N1 outbreak tended to affect younger, healthier people (six months to 24 years) disproportionately compared to typical seasonal influenza which hits infants, the elderly, and chronically ill people hardest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public-health messaging, vaccination, and clinical preparedness should account for the shifted age-risk profile of the pandemic strain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence review caveat on antiviral effectiveness in healthy adults
rubrics_metrics.description: The Cochrane Collaboration found oseltamivir offered mild benefits for healthy adults if taken within 24 hours of onset of symptoms, but found no clear evidence it prevented lower respiratory tract infections or other complications; overall there was a 'paucity of good data.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The evidence base for widespread antiviral benefits in healthy adults is limited; this affects recommendations about population-level antiviral use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antiviral resistance surveillance finding
rubrics_metrics.description: WHO reported that samples of the 2009 pandemic H1N1 flu had shown resistance to oseltamivir (Tamiflu) in some instances, while no circulating flu had yet shown resistance to zanamivir (Relenza).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resistance monitoring is essential to inform treatment recommendations and substitute agent selection.
